newsitem.title: USA: Swiss banks agree to panel on Holocaust claims.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks agree to panel on Holocaust claims.

text.p: Swiss banks have agreed to have Holocaust-era claims resolved by an independent panel and not by the banks themselves, a source close to U.S. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato said on Tuesday.

The decision is expected to be announced at a House of Representatives Banking Committee hearing on Wednesday but the source said there were still some details to be worked out on how the claims-arbitration panel would work.

The creation of an independent panel would represent a rare lifting of Swiss bank secrecy rules and remove the banks from deciding on the disposition of possibly thousands of accounts, the source said.

He added that the decision would mean that the heavily criticized Swiss Bank Ombudsman's office would either be downgraded or abolished. Jewish groups charge that the ombudsman has done little to return funds to Holocaust survivors or their heirs.
The office took in more than $100,000 in fees and was able to locate dormant accounts containing less than $9,000.

In addition, the Swiss have agreed to published the names of dormant accounts held by both foreigners and by Swiss nationals. During the war many Swiss nationals acted as go-betweens setting up accounts for Jews in Swiss banks.
Earlier this year, D'Amato called on Swiss banks to make public the names on all dormant accounts and set up a claims-resolution process.
For more than 50 years, heirs to funds deposited by Jews murdered in the Holocaust have accused Swiss banks of refusing to make their money available.

The heirs, many of whom are taking part in a class-action law suit against Swiss banks, said they were systematically refused their money because of bank demands for documentation -- including, in some cases, death certificates for people murdered in Hitler's death camps.

D'Amato and former Federal Reserve Board Chairman Paul Volcker are scheduled to testify at the House Banking Committee hearing. Volcker heads a special commission set up by the Swiss banks and Jewish groups trying to determine how much Holocaust-era deposits are still in Swiss banks.

The Volcker Commission was established after an international outcry over Swiss handling of deposits by Jews seeking a safe haven for their money. The Swiss instituted a system of secret bank accounts after the Nazis forbade Jews to have accounts in Germany.
The source said the independent panel will be set up in consultation with the Swiss and the Volcker commission.
Meanwhile, New York state banking authorities plan to set up a separate office to help claimants fill out forms, file claims and provide advise.
